description:
src/memory.rs:500-528 (update_object):

  // LIMITATION: Only top-level key patches are supported.  Paths using "/"
  // syntax (e.g. "keywords/flag1") are ignored — the key is merged as-is at
  // the top level of the serialized node.

The 'merged as-is' behavior means that a patch '{ "shareWith/alice": null }' produces a stored node with a top-level field named literally 'shareWith/alice' rather than mutating the nested shareWith map. The deserialization at line 531 then needs to parse the resulting node_val back into FileNode.

If FileNode has #[serde(deny_unknown_fields)], the deserialization will fail with 'unknown field shareWith/alice' and the patch will surface as Other(MemoryError). The client sees a confusing internal error.

If FileNode does NOT have deny_unknown_fields, the bogus field is silently dropped on deserialization and the patch silently no-ops without an error. The client thinks the update succeeded.

For the 'reference implementation' claim to hold, this must either:
(a) Implement RFC 8620 §5.3 PatchObject semantics correctly (JSON Pointer paths into nested maps).
(b) Return Err(BackendSetError::SetError(SetError::new(SetErrorType::InvalidPatch))) for any patch key containing '/'.

(b) is much smaller and fixes the silent-no-op case. (a) is the right long-term answer.

The current 'merged as-is' behavior is the worst of both worlds: looks like it works in tests with simple keys, silently breaks for any client that uses pointer paths.
title: MemoryBackend update_object documents 'LIMITATION: only top-level key patches are supported' but this is a silent correctness gap for non-trivial PatchObjects
